doc: The rules the route-detail screen applies to a route payload before anything is drawn: which stop the rider boarded at (`isOriginStop`), which arrivals count as upcoming (`upcoming`), which inferred buses are worth a token on the rail (`visibleBusMarkers`), and what the two ends of the route are called (`routeTerminusNames`). Three of the four are honesty judgements rather than data transformations — a bus parked at the terminus is not an arrival, a departed reading is not an arrival, and a circular route has no second terminus to name — so they are exactly the kind of thing a hand-port to Swift or Kotlin gets subtly wrong while still looking right. ISO arrival strings carry a fixed +08:00 offset; `nowIso` is the clock reading, always passed in, never read. Since WP6-6 it also carries `routeDetailView` — the whole screen composed in one call, which is where those four rules are actually joined.

isOriginStop.doc: Does a stop in the route sequence refer to the stop the rider opened this route from? The origin may be a merged same-kerb place id (`P:<a>+<b>+…`), in which case any of its poles counts.

cases.name: a-pole-of-the-origin-place-is-the-origin
cases.why: The common case on a merged kerb: the rider tapped a place, the route sequence names one pole of it. A port that compared the two ids directly would never find the boarding stop, so the here-anchor and its auto-scroll would silently stop working on exactly the busy stops where they matter most.

cases.name: the-last-member-of-a-four-member-place-still-counts
cases.why: Clustering has been N-member since ADR-042, so a rule that only looked at the first two members would pass a pair fixture and fail here.

cases.name: a-pole-across-the-road-is-not-the-origin
cases.why: The opposite kerb is a different place id and a different pole. Matching it would anchor the screen on the stop going the other way — the one mistake that makes the whole here-anchor untrustworthy.

cases.name: a-lone-pole-matches-itself
cases.why: A stop that was never merged has no place id at all. `memberStopIds` yields it unchanged, so there is no place/pole branch in this rule — the row that stops a port from adding one.

cases.name: no-origin-anchors-nothing
cases.why: The route screen is reachable without a boarding stop — from search, from a saved route, from a deep link. Every row must then read as an ordinary stop rather than the first one being highlighted by accident.

cases.name: a-blank-origin-anchors-nothing
cases.why: An empty string is what an absent query parameter degrades to on the way through a URL. It denotes no stop, so it must behave like no stop and not fall through to an id comparison against an empty string.

cases.name: a-malformed-place-id-denotes-no-pole
cases.why: `P:` with no members parses to nothing, and `memberStopIds` returns an empty list rather than the literal string. Nothing may match it — least of all a stop that happens to be called `P:`.

cases.name: an-unrecognised-origin-id-is-compared-as-itself
cases.why: An id we cannot parse is passed through opaquely rather than rejected: a grammar written today must not invalidate an id a rider saved yesterday that the dataset still resolves (ADR-052 durability).

upcoming.doc: The arrivals a stop row shows: not-yet-departed only, feed order preserved, capped at `maxArrivals`. The cap is served policy (ADR-053), not a constant: a row with no `maxArrivals` argument is stating the shipped default of three, and the last row states an override. These rows were pinned at a literal three until Wave 3, when the number moved to `ClientPolicy` so that the same question could stop being answered three different ways across the app — so they now pin the *rule* (filter first, then cap) and only incidentally the count.

cases.name: three-upcoming-arrivals-pass-through
cases.why: The ordinary shape. Nothing is reformatted or re-sorted here — the row exists so a port keeps this a filter and does not turn it into a parse-and-rebuild.

cases.name: the-fourth-arrival-is-dropped
cases.why: KMB publishes up to five readings per stop. The cap is applied AFTER the departed filter, so a departed first reading must not eat one of the three visible slots — which is what capping first would do.

cases.name: exactly-sixty-seconds-late-is-not-departed
cases.why: The tolerance band is inclusive at -60 s: the feed's clock and ours disagree by seconds, so a bus reported one minute ago is still 'Due', not gone. Matches `etaView.hasDeparted` exactly; a port that used `<=` here would blank a stop the rider is standing at.

cases.name: one-second-past-the-tolerance-is-departed
cases.why: The first second a stale reading disappears. Pinned next to the row above because the pair is the whole boundary.

cases.name: an-out-of-order-feed-is-not-re-sorted
cases.why: Deliberate. The operators publish soonest-first and the rest of the app reads `arrivals[0]` as the next bus, so re-sorting here would hide a feed that had stopped doing that in the one place a rider would have noticed. If this ever needs to change it changes for `dedupeEtas` and the bus markers too, not just for the display.

cases.name: no-eta-block-at-all
cases.why: Most stops on a long route carry no live reading, and the field is absent rather than empty. Absent must behave as empty and never as an error.

cases.name: every-reading-has-departed
cases.why: Late at night the last readings sit in the past for a while. The row shows no times rather than a row of dashes.

cases.name: a-served-cap-overrides-the-default
cases.why: The row that makes the cap policy rather than a constant (ADR-053). Same feed as `the-fourth-arrival-is-dropped`, a served cap of two, two arrivals out — and the departed first reading is still filtered before the cap applies, so overriding the number must not reorder the two steps. A port that read its own constant instead of the argument passes every other row in this group and fails only this one.

visibleBusMarkers.doc: Filters the markers `inferBusMarkers` produced: a bus still parked at the origin is furniture, not an arrival, and is only drawn once it is within `ORIGIN_BUS_DEPARTS_WITHIN_SEC` (120 s) of departing.

cases.name: origin-bus-119s-from-departing-is-drawn
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. One second inside the window. The three 119/120/121 rows are the whole rule: the threshold is a judgement about what counts as 'about to leave' (ADR-008), so it has to be pinned as a number rather than re-derived from whatever the label happens to say. A port that compared minutes instead of seconds would show this bus and the 121 s one identically, both reading '2 min'.

cases.name: origin-bus-exactly-120s-from-departing-is-drawn
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. The comparison is inclusive at the threshold. Off-by-one here costs one second of visibility and would never be noticed by eye, which is precisely why it is a fixture.

cases.name: origin-bus-121s-from-departing-is-suppressed
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. One second outside, and the token disappears. Every journey starts at stop 0, so without this the origin node carries a permanently parked bus that reads as one the rider could catch.

cases.name: an-origin-marker-with-no-arrival-is-suppressed
cases.why: Unreachable from `inferBusMarkers`, which only emits a marker where a live reading exists — but pinned because absent must mean absent. There is no departure time, so there is nothing to be within two minutes of, and drawing a token anyway would invent a bus from a missing field. A port that treated 'no reading' as 'not yet outside the window' would put a permanent bus on stop 0 of every route with no live data at all, which is most routes at night.

cases.name: an-origin-bus-due-now-is-drawn-on-the-node
cases.why: Inside the window and imminent, so `atStop` survives untouched. The suppression decides WHETHER a marker is drawn and never edits one — a port that recomputed `atStop` here would have two places deciding the same thing.

cases.name: buses-elsewhere-on-the-route-are-never-suppressed
cases.why: The rule is about stop 0 only. A bus twenty minutes from a mid-route stop is real information — that is the whole point of the rail — so nothing but the origin is judged against the window.

cases.name: a-parked-origin-bus-goes-and-the-one-on-the-road-stays
cases.why: The realistic shape mid-afternoon: a bus sitting at the terminus twelve minutes before it leaves, and one already running. Only the second is drawn, and the surviving marker keeps its own index — a port that filtered by rebuilding the list from positions would renumber it onto the wrong segment.

cases.name: no-markers-at-all
cases.why: A route with no live buses. Empty in, empty out, no index arithmetic on an empty list.

routeTerminusNames.doc: The two ends of a route as the header announces them: the stop list's first and last names when it has loaded, the route's own abbreviated labels until then, and a 'circular via' turnaround place instead of a second terminus when the route loops (ADR-046).

cases.name: stop-names-beat-the-route-labels
cases.why: The stop sequence has loaded, so the header uses the full stop names with their operator codes split off — richer than the LED-sign abbreviations the route carries. This is the ordinary case and it is also the one that proves the two sources are cleaned differently: a stop name loses its trailing code, a route label does not.

cases.name: the-display-locale-picks-the-name
cases.why: Every bus-data name is an `I18nText` and the locale is chosen here, once, rather than by each caller. The Chinese names carry no operator code and no Latin letters, so both the code split and the title-caser must leave them exactly as upstream wrote them.

cases.name: a-circular-route-whose-origin-is-also-its-destination
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW, and the reason this rule exists. A circular service ends where it began, so the first and last stops are the same pole and a faithful header would read 'Fuk Tsun Street -> Fuk Tsun Street' — true, and useless. The loop is flagged in the destination name itself, HK-style, so the far end becomes the turnaround place for a 'Circular via …' line and the marker itself is stripped out of it. A port that only compared the first and last stop ids would miss the many circulars whose sequence starts and ends at adjacent poles.

cases.name: the-loop-marker-is-read-in-english-and-stripped-in-the-display-locale
cases.why: Two different fields in one rule: the '(CIRCULAR)' flag is looked for in `en` because that is the field the three feeds spell consistently, while the place shown to the rider comes from the display locale and loses its own '(循環線)' suffix. A port that detected and stripped in the same locale would either miss the loop on a Chinese UI or leave the marker in the rendered name.

cases.name: a-blank-english-destination-hides-the-loop
cases.why: WRONG, and recorded so all three platforms are wrong in the same way. Upstream really ships GMB circulars with a blank `en` while the Chinese reads '大角咀(循環線)' — the same blank the search corpus pins. The marker is looked for in `en`, so the loop goes undetected and the header falls back to the last stop, reading '福全街 -> 福全街': exactly the uselessness the circular rule exists to prevent, for the rider most likely to be on this route. Fixing it means detecting the marker in whichever name is present rather than in `en` alone, at which point `expect` becomes an origin of '福全街' and a destination of { kind: circular, via: '大角咀' }. Left as-is here because the fix belongs with the stop-name rules, not with the header.

cases.name: before-the-stops-load-the-route-labels-stand-in
cases.why: The header paints before the stop sequence arrives, and an empty header that then fills in is worse than an abbreviated one that sharpens. The fallback must NOT be run through the stop-code splitter: '(CITY ONE)' is part of the place, not an operator code, so a port that reused the stop-name cleaner here would silently amputate half the label.

cases.name: a-circular-route-before-its-stops-load
cases.why: The loop is known from the route payload alone, so the 'Circular via …' treatment must appear on the first paint rather than after the sequence arrives — otherwise the header visibly changes shape under the rider's eyes.

cases.name: nothing-has-loaded-yet
cases.why: Both sources absent — the first frame after navigation, and the error state. Blank strings, so the header lays out at its normal height and nothing jumps when the data lands. Never the word 'undefined', which is what a naive template produces.

cases.name: stops-without-a-route-payload
cases.why: Possible while a direction flip swaps the payload underneath a kept-previous stop list. The names still come from the stops, and no loop is claimed — the marker lives on the route, so with no route there is nothing to read it from.

cases.name: a-single-stop-route-is-its-own-terminus
cases.why: A one-row sequence, which happens on a truncated or special-departure pattern. First and last are the same element, and the rule must not index past the end to find a second one.

routeDetailView.doc: The whole Route screen in one call: the header’s two labels, the static-facts strip, every stop row with its readouts and its saved star, the buses on the rail placed by stop index, the boarding anchor, and the route’s straight-line distance. Sixteen decisions that lived in `apps/mobile/app/route/[id].tsx`, `RouteMeta.tsx` and `RouteHeader.tsx` as loose expressions (WP6-6a). `labels` is a fixture supplied by each platform’s suite, never the app’s catalogue — what these rows pin is the COMPOSITION: where the arrow goes, which fact is a note rather than a pill, and which node a bus is on. `now` is a clock reading passed in.

cases.name: a-route-opened-from-a-stop-anchors-that-row
cases.why: The ordinary arrival from Place detail: `?stop=` names a pole in the sequence, so that row is the anchor and `hereIndex` is what the reveal’s second beat scrolls to. A port that only set the row’s own flag would emphasise the right row and scroll to the wrong one — the two facts are the same fact, which is why one call produces both.

buses.label: Bus approaching Tin Shui Wai Park

cases.name: a-merged-place-anchors-on-any-of-its-poles
cases.why: The rider tapped a merged same-kerb place, so `?stop=` is a `P:` id and the sequence names one member of it. This is `isOriginStop` reached through the composition rather than on its own, which is the level a renderer actually calls — the row that stops a port from comparing the two ids directly and silently losing the anchor on exactly the busy stops where it matters most.

cases.name: a-flip-drops-the-anchor-even-when-the-reverse-serves-the-same-pole
cases.why: THE ROW THAT MAKES `flipped` A SEPARATE ARGUMENT. Once the rider has flipped, the stop they arrived at belongs to the direction they left — the reverse serves the opposite kerbs. Deriving "flipped" from "did the id match" would keep an anchor on a route whose reverse happens to name the same pole, which is a real shape (a terminus is often one pole for both bounds) and would emphasise a row the rider never boarded at. The payload carries its `reverse`, because a route with nowhere to flip to cannot reach this state at all — which is what makes it drivable by pressing the toggle rather than by setting a flag.

cases.name: an-origin-bus-nearly-leaving-rides-the-first-node
cases.why: Two rules composed, and the composition is what a renderer cannot be trusted with: `visibleBusMarkers` lets an origin bus through only because it is within two minutes of leaving, and then it is drawn ON stop 0’s node because stop 0 has no segment leading into it. A port that applied only the second would park a permanent token at every terminus; one that applied only the first would try to draw a bus on a segment that does not exist.

buses.label: Bus at Tin Shui Wai Station

cases.name: an-origin-bus-not-yet-leaving-earns-no-token
cases.why: The same payload eight minutes earlier in the bus’s day: the feed reports the terminus departure long before anyone can board it, so the token is furniture that reads as a bus a rider could catch (ADR-008). The rail is empty and the row still shows the time — which is the honest split, and is invisible unless the suppression is asserted through the view rather than only on its own function.

cases.name: a-bus-mid-route-rides-the-segment-leading-into-its-stop
cases.why: The common case, and the one the schematic exists for. It carries BOTH of `inferBusMarkers`’ discontinuities at once, which is why it has two tokens and not one: stop 3’s predecessor has no reading at all (one bus), and stop 4’s reading is SOONER than stop 3’s, so the lead bus has already passed stop 3 (a second bus). Each is drawn midway between two nodes — `from`/`to` rather than a y, because where those nodes are on screen is geometry: a 52 px RN rail and a DOM list whose rows measure themselves must agree about the bus and are free to disagree about the pixels.

cases.name: a-bus-a-minute-away-stands-on-the-node-it-is-reaching
cases.why: `atStop` is `isDue`, so a bus under the "Due" band is drawn on the node rather than on the approach — the token and the word the row prints are the same judgement, and `dueUnderSec` is the one threshold both read. Recorded because a port that placed every non-origin bus on a segment would show a bus still approaching a stop whose row says it is here.

cases.name: a-circular-route-heads-its-own-loop-line-and-offers-no-toggle
cases.why: A loop ends where it began, so "A → A" tells a rider nothing and an arrow pointing at the loop line reads as travelling *to* the loop. Both header labels collapse to the one sentence, `circular` is set, and there is no `reverseId` — three facts a renderer previously derived separately in `RouteHeader`, where a `circular ?` branch was written twice.

cases.name: a-bidirectional-route-carries-the-id-its-toggle-navigates-to
cases.why: The toggle’s existence and the id it flips to are ONE field. The RN screen held them as `canReverse={!!reverse}` beside a separate closure reading `reverse.id`, so a renderer could draw a control with nothing behind it — and the DOM port, which navigates rather than swapping state, needs the id at the point it draws the control.

cases.name: the-whole-screen-is-composed-in-the-readers-own-locale
cases.why: The same payload in `zh-Hant`, which is where a port most easily reads one locale and prints another: the header, both its labels and every row name come from the Chinese names, and `formatHeadway` says 每 … 分鐘 while `formatServiceHours` — a clock span — is identical in all three. It also pins a **cross-locale asymmetry that is real and already explained**: `splitStopCode` understands ASCII parentheses only (`stop-name.spec.json` says why — widening it would only ever produce a false split on a Chinese name), so the English row splits `CENTRAL (EXCHANGE SQUARE)` into a label and a "code" while the Chinese keeps `中環（交易廣場）` whole. Two renderers must render that identically; a port that normalised the brackets would silently disagree with this one on 167 poles.

header.label: 天水圍站 → 中環（交易廣場）

cases.name: an-empty-sequence-still-names-the-route-from-its-own-labels
cases.why: The first paint after a cold open: the route document has arrived and the stop list has not, or the dataset has a route with no sequence at all. The header falls back to the route’s abbreviated labels rather than flashing empty, there is no stop-count pill (a "0 stops" fact states a route length we do not believe), and `distanceM` is 0 rather than a guess.

cases.name: the-fare-pill-falls-back-from-a-sectional-span-to-the-origin-fare
cases.why: HK fares are sectional and the span is framed dearest → cheapest, because boarding later costs less. A route whose stops carry no per-stop fares still has one number worth printing (`service.fareFull`), and that fallback lived in `RouteMeta.tsx` where a second renderer would have had to find it. Both halves are in the corpus: this row has no per-stop fares, the rows above have them.

cases.name: a-holiday-fare-is-a-note-on-the-fare-pill-never-a-pill-of-its-own
cases.why: Upstream publishes `fareFullHoliday` only when it differs. It qualifies the fare rather than standing beside it as a fifth fact, and the qualifier word is the catalogue’s (`labels.holiday`) while the `$` and the space are the kernel’s — the composition is exactly what two renderers get subtly different.

cases.name: a-route-with-no-service-block-has-no-facts-strip-at-all
cases.why: A real state, not a defensive branch: the dataset carries routes with no service facts, and a strip of nothing is furniture. `facts` is empty rather than four pills reading "—", so a renderer draws no strip at all — and, because the strip is the schematic’s first child, this is also the case where a port’s measured row offsets differ from every other case.

cases.name: a-saved-route-stars-only-the-pole-it-was-saved-at
cases.why: A favourite is a route AT A POLE (ADR-042), so starring every row of a saved route would claim the rider had saved five stops. The key is `formatFavoriteRouteKey`’s and is built from the row’s RAW pole id — the same id `?pole=` carries and the same one `favouritesView` reads back — which is what keeps this screen’s star and the Favourites tab’s list talking about one thing.

buses.label: Bus approaching Tin Shui Wai Park

cases.name: a-stale-board-dims-every-slot-on-its-row-together
cases.why: Staleness is the BOARD’s, not the arrival’s: one `dataTimestamp` per stop, so all three slots carry the same `stale` and dim together. A per-slot answer would make the third time look fresher than the first, which is precision this app does not have (ADR-008). The neighbouring row is fresh in the same case, so a port that stamped the whole view goes red.

buses.label: Bus approaching Tin Shui Wai Park

cases.name: a-departed-reading-is-not-an-arrival-and-leaves-its-row-with-nothing
cases.why: Upstream republishes about once a minute, so a reading for a bus that has already gone is common rather than exotic. The row keeps its name and its fare and shows no time — which is what "we have nothing to say" looks like here — and the rail draws no token for it, because `inferBusMarkers` nulls departed readings BEFORE the discontinuity scan.

cases.name: a-served-policy-caps-the-arrivals-and-moves-the-due-band-with-them
cases.why: The cap is `ClientPolicy.maxArrivals` (ADR-053), served rather than compiled in, and this is the row that stops a port hard-coding three: four readings appear as two. The soonest is **45 seconds away**, which is deliberate — under the shipped 60 s band it would read "Due", and under this case’s served `dueUnderSec: 30` it reads as a figure. So the row fails a port that honours the served cap and quietly keeps the compiled-in band, which is the exact defect `etaLabelParts` was given a `dueUnderSec` argument to close (ADR-053 consequences).

buses.label: Bus at Tin Shui Wai Park

cases.name: a-sparse-service-block-yields-only-the-facts-it-can-support
cases.why: The dataset carries routes whose service block has a journey time and nothing else — no fare of any kind, no headway band, no service span. Each pill is present only where its datum is, so this route’s strip is the stop count alone. The row exists because the alternative is four pills reading "—", which is the Static tier claiming facts it does not have (ADR-036) — and because a port with a fixed four-pill layout passes every other case in this group.

cases.name: a-citybus-route-says-its-times-are-per-stop-rather-than-reading-as-empty
cases.why: The defect ADR-114 closed, kept as the row that proves it stays closed. `/v1/route/:id` fetches live arrivals for KMB and LWB only — Citybus publishes no bulk route-eta endpoint at all (ADR-021) and GMB is not wired either — so on a CTB or GMB route EVERY row carries `eta: null`, for ever. That is unchanged and correct; what was wrong is that the view said nothing about it, so the screen rendered exactly what "no bus is due right now" renders and a rider could not tell a route the app never asks about from a route with nothing coming. `liveArrivals: perStopOnly` is the answer, and note what it is NOT: not an `EtaFailure[]` like `/v1/nearby` carries, because a route is one upstream call and naming 34 poles would invent a granularity the fetch does not have. The screen says it once.

cases.name: a-round-the-route-feed-did-not-answer-is-not-a-route-with-no-buses
cases.why: The other half of ADR-114, and the half that belongs to the biggest operator. `/v1/route/:id` wraps the KMB route-eta fetch in `.catch(() => [])` — deliberately, because a route view without live times is still a route view: the stop list, the geometry and the fares are all static and erroring the screen would lose them (ADR-073). What the catch also did was make an upstream outage indistinguishable from a quiet route, on KMB, where every rider is. `liveArrivals: unavailable` is the difference, and it is a different sentence from `perStopOnly` because it is worth retrying and that one never will be. Note what survives: the facts strip is intact, which is the whole reason the catch is there.

cases.name: a-live-route-watch-fills-the-rows-a-citybus-route-cannot-fill-itself
cases.why: What a rider sees once `/v1/live?route=` is answering (ADR-116): the per-stop times are there, the screen-level notice is gone because an absent `liveArrivals` IS 'answered', and the one kerb whose board refused says so on its own row rather than reading as a stop with no bus due. The payload is exactly what `applyLiveEtasToRouteDetail` produces, so the two rules are pinned against one document.

routeFactSheet.doc: One of the four fact sheets a static pill opens (ADR-044), derived once: the sectional-fare timeline with its concession estimates, the per-day-type frequency bands, the first/last hours, and the whole-route overview. Eight decisions that lived in `apps/mobile/components/RouteFactSheets.tsx` (WP6-6c) — which is why that file was the one surface `check-no-derivation` still did not police. `labels` is a fixture supplied by each platform’s suite; what these rows pin is the COMPOSITION, chiefly the `~` that marks an estimate and the ` · ` that joins an unnamed day mask. `view` is `routeDetailView`’s output for the same payload, so a timeline cannot name a stop differently from the schematic above it.

cases.name: the-fare-timeline-steps-down-and-names-where-you-board-for-each-price
cases.why: The sheet ADR-044 exists for. HK fares are **sectional**, so a rider boarding later pays less, and the timeline says where each price starts and how far it carries them. The boarding name comes from the schematic’s own rows rather than a second mapping — the route screen used to build a third list here with `titleCaseName(splitStopCode(…).label)`, one edit away from a timeline that named its stages differently from the list above it (WP6-6a).

cases.name: every-fare-stage-carries-both-concession-estimates-or-neither
cases.why: Both or neither, because both come from the same parse. Two independent optionals would let a renderer draw a child figure beside a missing elderly one, which reads as "no elderly concession on this route" rather than "we could not work it out". Each figure carries its own `~`: these are policy-derived estimates, not route data, and ADR-008 forbids presenting an estimate as a reading — so the mark that says so is composed here where one renderer cannot drop it.

cases.name: a-route-whose-fares-are-not-numbers-opens-an-entirely-blank-fare-sheet
cases.why: A LIVE DEFECT, and the row records it as it stands. `fareStages` skips any fare it cannot read as a number (its own guard, `Number.isNaN(Number(f))`), so a payload whose per-stop fares are non-numeric yields **no stages at all** — and `concessions` is empty with them, which is correct on its own terms: there is no estimate to make and a legend keyed to figures that are not on screen is worse than none. What makes it a defect is the pill: `fareRange` skips the same values, falls back to `service.fareFull`, and the strip therefore reads `$13.4`. So a rider taps a pill showing a fare and gets a blank sheet. WHEN FIXED: the sheet falls back to the origin full fare as a single stage covering the whole route — the same datum the pill used — and says nothing about sections it cannot describe. Owner: `docs/07`. Whether upstream actually publishes such a fare is not something this row measures; the guard makes the state reachable by construction, which is enough to pin it.

cases.name: a-sequence-that-does-not-start-at-one-still-names-the-right-boarding-stops
cases.why: THE ROW THAT MAKES THE LOOKUP A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. `fareStages` numbers its stages from the **array** it was handed (`fromSeq` is `index + 1`), while a row’s `seq` is what the **wire** numbered it — and `RouteStopRowView.seq`’s own note says the two agree today and would differ on a payload whose sequence was offset or gapped. So the boarding stop is looked up by **position**, and this payload (seq 5…9) is what tells the two apart: by position it names Tin Shui Wai Station and Kingswood Richly Plaza, and by `seq` it would find no row at all and print blank headings above real prices. Written after an injection that reverted the lookup came back **green** — every other fixture has `seq === index + 1`, so the fix was reasoning rather than a measurement until this row existed.

cases.name: the-frequency-sheet-breaks-the-coarse-pill-into-its-own-bands
cases.why: The pill says "every 10 – 25 min" because that is all a pill can honestly say; this sheet is where the peak band that produced the 10 and the off-peak one that produced the 25 are visible. A single-headway band is formatted as a **degenerate range** rather than by a second rule, which is what keeps "every 4 min" here and "every 10 – 25 min" on the pill in one voice.

cases.name: without-a-frequency-table-the-sheet-falls-back-to-the-coarse-range
cases.why: Most of the dataset. The fallback is the same string the pill shows, and it appears **only** when there is no table — a sheet that showed both would state one fact twice at two fidelities and invite a rider to wonder which is right.

cases.name: with-neither-a-table-nor-a-range-the-frequency-sheet-is-empty
cases.why: Reachable, which is the point: the pill that opens this sheet is the **stop count**’s in that case, so a route with no frequency data at all can still get here. Empty rather than a placeholder — the Static tier shows what the open data says (ADR-036).

cases.name: the-hours-sheet-gives-each-day-type-its-own-first-and-last
cases.why: The coarse span on the pill is the earliest first and the latest last across every day type, so a rider reading "05:30 – 00:15" cannot tell that Sunday starts 40 minutes later. This sheet is where the true edges are, per day type, and the times are printed as upstream publishes them (a "24:15" is a service that runs past midnight, not a typo).

cases.name: without-a-pattern-table-the-hours-sheet-falls-back-to-the-coarse-span
cases.why: The same fallback rule as the frequency sheet, and it is stated as its own row rather than assumed symmetric: the two sheets read different fields of the same block, and a port that wired one fallback and forgot the other would look right on every route that has patterns.

cases.name: an-unnamed-day-mask-is-named-by-the-days-it-runs
cases.why: THE COMPOSITION IN THIS GROUP. `dayType: "other"` means the dataset’s mask matches none of the four named types, and the honest answer is to name the days — **Sunday-first, in the mask’s own order, joined with the app’s separator**. That was `.map().filter(Boolean).join(" · ")` in a renderer: three decisions (which days, in what order, with what between them) for one answer, and a second renderer would have picked a comma.

cases.name: a-mask-that-names-no-days-falls-back-to-the-generic-word
cases.why: The other side of the composition, and it is not defensive: an all-false mask is a pattern the dataset carries and nobody can describe, so the generic word is the only honest label. A port that joined an empty list would print an empty heading above a real band table.

cases.name: the-overview-states-the-stop-count-the-journey-and-the-distance
cases.why: Three whole-route figures, each present only where the dataset supports it, and each flagged for whether it is an **estimate** — because one of them is a straight-line sum through the stops (there are no polylines upstream) and one is upstream’s own timing. A renderer that treated them alike would either over- or under-claim. `estimate` is a flag rather than a `~` in the string because the caveat under it is a whole sentence the catalogue owns.

cases.name: the-overview-omits-a-journey-time-the-dataset-does-not-carry
cases.why: A service block with no `journeyMin`, which is common. The row is absent rather than "—": a figure we do not have is not a figure. The stop count survives, because it is what the pill counted.

cases.name: a-route-with-no-stops-still-states-a-stop-count-of-zero
cases.why: The one figure that is always present, and deliberately: this sheet was opened from the count pill, and a rider who tapped a number expects to see it. Zero is also honest — the distance is dropped (a straight line through nothing is not zero metres, it is no answer) and so is the journey time, and a corpus row is the only way that asymmetry stays deliberate.

cases.name: the-whole-sheet-is-composed-in-the-readers-own-locale
cases.why: The frequency sheet in `zh-Hant`: `formatHeadway` says 每 … 分鐘 while `formatServiceHours` — a clock span — is identical in every locale. The day names are the caller’s and the separator between them is the kernel’s, which is the split that keeps a Chinese heading from being joined with an English comma.

routeStopBoard.doc: This route’s next arrivals at ONE pole, read out of that pole’s own board — what the action sheet fetches on demand when the route view has no times of its own (Citybus and GMB, ADR-114/115). Three decisions: the formatting is the schematic row’s so a time cannot read two ways, `incomplete` is `failed`’s rather than an empty list’s, and which of a report’s readings belongs to THIS pole when a place has two kerbs on one route.

cases.name: two-kerbs-of-one-place-take-the-pole-that-was-asked-about
cases.why: A board requested for a pole may be resolved to its place (ADR-042), so one route can appear twice at two kerbs — and on a schematic those are different rows. The exact `stopId` wins.

cases.name: a-single-reading-answers-the-question-that-was-asked
cases.why: The alias table can promote the requested id, so the reading comes back under the place’s spelling. One reading for the route is unambiguously the answer to the question we asked; two are not.

cases.name: a-pole-whose-board-did-not-answer-is-incomplete-rather-than-empty
cases.why: ADR-077, one level down: no readings and nothing due are different sentences, and the sheet must not say "no bus due" about a board that refused us.
